title: Choose an internal table by the operation
scenario: Three orders arrive as 9/B/90, 3/A/30 and 5/A/50 (ID/customer/amount). Compare STANDARD with EMPTY KEY, SORTED by customer and ID, and HASHED by unique ID. The interactive example also lets you add order 7/A/70.
goal: Match the declared key and table category to the access pattern without inventing performance timings.

steps.title: Start with the same rows
steps.explanation: The fixture appends IDs 9, 3 and 5 in that order. A STANDARD table with EMPTY KEY preserves that insertion order here. SORTED keeps the declared customer-plus-ID order. HASHED offers no index-based order contract.
steps.outcome: These are in-memory example rows, not a database query.

steps.title: Choose the lookup you need
steps.explanation: For ID 9, HASHED can use its complete unique key. ID alone is not the leading part of this SORTED key. For all customer-A orders, the leading customer part of the sorted key is useful.
steps.outcome: A table category alone does not tell you whether a particular access is optimized.

steps.title: Read or insert a row
steps.explanation: ID 9 returns the B order for 90. Customer A returns IDs 3 and 5. Adding ID 7/A/70 appends it in the STANDARD fixture; SORTED places it with customer A. HASHED admits its new unique ID but has no promised display position.
steps.outcome: Changing a scene option starts again from the same three-row fixture.

steps.title: Explain the trade-off
steps.explanation: Use STANDARD for this arrival-order sequence, SORTED for the customer-key group, or HASHED for the exact unique-ID lookup. Scanning customer A in the hashed table does not receive its full-key lookup advantage. Real choices also depend on writes, secondary keys, memory and measured workloads.
steps.outcome: The animation illustrates the access contract, not SAP kernel internals or a benchmark.

takeaway: Choose the operation first, then a table category and key that support it.
limitation: A tiny illustrative fixture with no secondary keys. Sorted-key access depends on the supplied leading key components. HASHED card positions are only a presentation choice. No runtime measurements or actual ABAP execution are shown.
